title: The engineer who inspected your building wants the repair job, too. What Florida condo law says about that
seoTitle: Florida Condo Inspector Bidding on Repairs: Disclosure Rules
description: Can the firm that did your Florida condo's milestone inspection or SIRS bid on the repairs? Yes, with written disclosure. Here is what the law requires.
dek: The person who finds the problem and the person who gets paid to fix it can be the same. Florida law doesn't ban that. It says the board has to be told, in writing, before anyone signs.
facebook: What if the engineer who wrote your building's repair list also wants to be paid for the repairs? Florida condo law says that has to be disclosed to the board in writing, and a contract can be voided if it wasn't. Here's how the rule works.

body.text: Here is a common moment at a condo board table. The engineer's report comes back with a list of repairs. A week later, a proposal arrives to do some of that work, and it comes from the same firm, or from a company with ties to it.

Is that allowed? In Florida, the short answer is yes, but only out in the open. The law requires written disclosure to the association. If the disclosure is missing, the association can end the contract. This article explains the rules in plain words, using the 2026 Florida Statutes. It is a guide, not legal advice. The association attorney is the right person for questions about your building.

body.title: Terms to know
body.text: Milestone inspection: a structural inspection of a condo building by a licensed architect or engineer, required by section 553.899 of Florida law, to check the safety of the building's load-bearing parts. SIRS (structural integrity reserve study): a study of the building's major parts, such as roof, structure and waterproofing, that sets how much the association must save for them. Design professional: under Florida law, a licensed architect, landscape architect, engineer, surveyor or geologist, or a registered interior designer. Relative: in these sections, a relative within the third degree of blood or marriage. Voidable: a contract that is valid until one side chooses to cancel it.
The milestone inspection rule
Section 553.899(12) has two parts.

First, an architect or engineer who bids to perform a milestone inspection must tell the association, in writing, if he or she intends to bid on any maintenance, repair or replacement work the inspection may recommend. That notice comes at the bidding stage, before the inspection is done.

Second, a design professional or a licensed contractor who bids on work the inspection recommended may not have a direct or indirect interest in the inspection firm, or be a relative of someone who does, unless that relationship is disclosed to the association in writing.

If the required written disclosure was not given, the law says the contract for services "is voidable and terminates upon the association filing a written notice terminating the contract." The professional or contractor may also face discipline under the law that licenses his or her profession.
The same rule for the SIRS

The condo law has a matching rule for structural integrity reserve studies, in section 718.112(2)(g). Any design professional or licensed contractor who bids to do a SIRS must disclose in writing any intent to bid on maintenance, repair or replacement work the study may recommend. A design professional or contractor bidding on work the SIRS recommended may not have an interest in the firm that did the study, or be a relative of someone who does, unless that is disclosed in writing.
The result for missing disclosure is the same: the contract is voidable and ends when the association files a written notice terminating it, and the professional may face discipline.

Notice what these rules do not say. They do not ban the inspector or the study firm from doing the work. They do not tell the board whom to hire. They make sure the board knows about the relationship before it decides.
When the conflict is on the board itself

A separate law, section 718.3027, covers conflicts of interest for the association's own directors and officers. They, and their relatives, must disclose to the board any activity that may reasonably be seen as a conflict. The law presumes a conflict if, without the required notice, a director or officer or a relative signs a contract with the association, or holds an interest in a business that works with the association or proposes to.

When that happens, the proposed deal must be listed on the meeting agenda, with the contracts attached. The director with the interest may make a presentation, then must leave during the discussion and the vote, and must not vote. Approval takes a vote of two-thirds of the other directors present. At the next owners' meeting, the deal must be disclosed, and any owner can move to bring it to a vote. A majority of the owners present can cancel it. If it is canceled, the association owes only the reasonable value of what was provided up to then, with no termination fee or penalty.

A director's contract that was not properly disclosed is voidable. It ends when a written notice terminating it, with the consent of at least 20 percent of the voting interests, is filed with the board.
What about getting other bids?

Section 718.3026 says that when a contract for materials, equipment or services will cost more than 5 percent of the association's total yearly budget, including reserves, the association must get competitive bids. It does not have to take the lowest bid. Contracts for engineering and architect services are not covered by this bidding rule, and there are exceptions for emergencies and for a business that is the only source of supply in the county.
What to do
If you are an owner:

items: When a repair contract shows up on a board agenda, ask in writing whether the contractor or design firm has any tie to the firm that did the milestone inspection or SIRS.
Ask whether any written disclosure was received, and when, and ask to see it.
If a board member or a relative is part of the deal, look for it on the agenda with the contract attached, and watch for the disclosure at the next owners' meeting.
For questions about whether the rules were followed, you can contact the state's Division of Condominiums or the Condominium Ombudsman's office for information.

body.text: If you are a board member:

items: When you hire an engineer or architect for a milestone inspection or SIRS, ask up front, in writing, whether the firm plans to bid on any recommended work.
Before signing any repair contract, ask each bidder in writing about any interest in, or family tie to, the inspection or study firm. Keep the answers with the contract.
Check whether the job crosses the 5 percent competitive-bid line in section 718.3026.
If a director or a relative has an interest, follow the agenda, recusal and two-thirds vote steps in section 718.3027.
Ask the association attorney to review any repair contract tied to the inspector before you sign, not after.

faq.q: Can the engineer who did my condo's milestone inspection also do the repairs in Florida?
faq.a: The law does not ban it. Section 553.899(12) requires the architect or engineer who bids on the inspection to disclose in writing any intent to bid on the repair work. A contractor or design professional with an interest in, or a family tie to, the inspection firm must also disclose it in writing.

faq.q: What happens if a Florida condo contractor didn't disclose a tie to the inspection firm?
faq.a: The contract is voidable. It ends when the association files a written notice terminating it. The contractor or design professional may also face discipline under his or her profession's licensing law.

faq.q: Can the company that did our SIRS bid on the repairs?
faq.a: Yes, if it discloses in writing. Section 718.112(2)(g) requires anyone bidding on a SIRS to disclose any intent to bid on recommended repairs, and anyone bidding on the repairs to disclose any interest in, or family tie to, the firm that did the study.

faq.q: Can a Florida condo board member's company get an association contract?
faq.a: Only with the steps in section 718.3027: disclosure, the deal listed on the agenda with the contract attached, the director leaving the discussion and vote, and approval by two-thirds of the other directors present. Owners can vote to cancel it at the next members' meeting.

faq.q: Does a Florida condo association have to get competitive bids for repairs?
faq.a: For contracts costing more than 5 percent of the total yearly budget, including reserves, yes, with some exceptions such as emergencies. The association does not have to accept the lowest bid. Engineering and architect services are exempt from this rule.
